questions.q: In the real simulation run, what was the exact probability P(return < -10%) computed independently via the normal CDF, and how did the N=1,000,000-sample estimate compare?
options: Exact ≈0.12854; the N=1,000,000 estimate (0.12745) was close but still slightly below it
Exact ≈0.5000; the N=1,000,000 estimate matched it exactly
Exact ≈0.0000; the simulation never found any losses
Exact ≈1.0000; every sample showed a loss
questions.explain: The independently computed exact value via the normal CDF was ≈0.12854, and the largest simulation (N=1,000,000) reached 0.12745 -- close, but not perfectly converged, consistent with the gradual 1/sqrt(N) convergence rate.

questions.q: What does the 1/sqrt(N) convergence rate imply about improving a Monte Carlo estimate's precision by a factor of 10?
options: It requires roughly 100 times as many samples
It requires roughly 10 times as many samples
It requires roughly the square root of 10 times as many samples
It requires no additional samples at all
questions.explain: Since error shrinks as 1/sqrt(N), improving precision by 10x requires increasing N by 10^2 = 100x -- this quadratic sample-count growth is exactly what motivates quantum amplitude estimation's alternative scaling in Lesson 16.

questions.q: What specifically does 'quantum Monte Carlo' (in the amplitude-estimation sense used in this course) change about the classical Monte Carlo pipeline?
options: It accelerates only the sampling/estimation step using quantum amplitude estimation, while the underlying probabilistic model (the return distribution, correlations, etc.) stays exactly the same
It replaces the entire financial model with a more sophisticated quantum model of asset returns
It eliminates the need for any probabilistic model of portfolio returns
It is unrelated to amplitude estimation and refers only to a classical physics technique
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that 'quantum Monte Carlo' in this financial context refers only to accelerating the estimation step via amplitude estimation -- the probabilistic model itself (step 1 of the classical pipeline) is unchanged.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the simulation estimates as sample count increased from 1,000 to 1,000,000?
options: The estimates (0.12600, 0.12490, 0.12736, 0.12745) got closer to the exact value overall, though not in a perfectly monotonic step-by-step fashion
The estimates decreased steadily and monotonically at every step with no exceptions
The estimates stayed exactly constant regardless of sample count
The estimates diverged further from the exact value as sample count grew
questions.explain: The estimates generally tightened toward the exact value of ≈0.12854 as N grew, though the convergence wasn't perfectly monotonic at every step -- exactly the kind of 'noisy early, tightening later' behavior the 1/sqrt(N) law predicts for a random process.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say classical Monte Carlo's cost structure becomes expensive for regulatory-grade, tight-tolerance risk calculations?
options: Because achieving much tighter precision requires quadratically more samples (via the 1/sqrt(N) law), so regulatory capital calculations demanding precision to within 0.1% can require enormous sample counts
Because classical computers cannot generate more than 1,000 random samples total
Because Monte Carlo simulation only works for portfolios with exactly one asset
Because the normal distribution cannot be sampled on classical hardware
questions.explain: Because precision improves only as the square root of sample count, demanding very tight precision (like regulatory capital requirements) requires proportionally enormous sample counts -- exactly the gap that motivates looking at amplitude estimation's quadratically better scaling in Lesson 16.
